articles.title: Divisão da direita pode fortalecer Alcolumbre na disputa pelo comando do Senado, avaliam aliados  | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente do Senado quer usar controle das emendas parlamentares para angariar votos para seguir no cargo
articles.summary: Presidente do Senado quer usar controle das emendas parlamentares para angariar votos para seguir no cargo
articles.body:
presidente do Senado Federal, senador Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP). — Foto: Ton Molina/Agência Senado

O presidente do Senado Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP) trabalha nos bastidores para se reeleger para o cargo que ocupa em fevereiro de 2027.

E, na visão de aliados, a divisão da direita entre Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) e Tereza Cristina (PP-MS) pode fortalecê-lo, com o possível apoio de senadores do grupo político do candidato do PL e da candidata do PP.

Na última semana, Alcolumbre entregou a relatoria do Projeto de Lei Orçamentária Anual (PLOA) para o líder do MDB, Eduardo Braga (AM), e o da Lei de Diretrizes Orçamentárias (LDO) para Eduardo Gomes (PL-TO), seu atual vice-presidente.

A escolha de Gomes ocorreu após Tereza recusar a relatoria para marcar posição como candidata.

Aliados de primeira hora de Alcolumbre, Braga e Gomes terão à mão um ativo para atrair o apoio de novos senadores: o controle das emendas parlamentares.

Alcolumbre aposta principalmente em ter sob seu domínio as emendas de comissão e as não-obrigatórias.

No orçamento deste ano, as emendas de comissão somaram um total de R$ 12,1 bilhões, sendo R$ 8,07 bilhões para a Câmara dos Deputados e R$ 4,03 bilhões para o Senado.

Diferentemente das emendas individuais e de bancada, as emendas de comissão não são impositivas, ou seja, o governo não é obrigado a pagar.

Ma, após ter articulado o avanço de pautas prioritárias do Executivo durante o período eleitoral, como as Propostas de Emenda à Constituição (PECs) do fim da escala 6x1 e da Segurança, Alcolumbre conta com o aval do governo alocar esses recursos.

Essa modalidade, que surgiu após o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) declarar inconstitucional as emendas de relator, conhecidas como orçamento secreto, mantém na cúpula do Congresso Nacional o controle do dinheiro.

Por escolher o relator da PLOA, o presidente costuma alinhar para quais comissões vão essas emendas, levando em conta principalmente que ministério será o responsável por liberar o recurso.

Em 2026, por exemplo, os R$ 4,03 bilhões do Senado foram divididos da seguinte forma:

R$ 2,1 bilhões para a Comissão de Assuntos Sociais (CAS)

R$ 1,5 bilhão para a Comissão de Desenvolvimento Regional e Turismo (CDR)

R$ 400 milhões para a Comissão de Agricultura (CRA)

À frente dessas comissões estão aliados de primeira hora de Alcolumbre. A CAS é comandada por Marcelo Castro (MDB-PI), a CDR pela senadora Dorinha Seabra (União-TO) e a CRA tem na presidência Zequinha Marinho (PL-PA).

Além de contar com aliados à frente dos colegiados responsáveis por votar a destinação dos recursos, Alcolumbre também poderá direcionar esse dinheiro para ministérios comandados por pessoas próximas a ele.

Por exemplo, os R$ 2,1 bilhões da CAS serão liberados pelo Fundo Nacional de Saúde (FNS), ligado ao Ministério da Saúde, comandado por Alexandre Padilha, com quem Alcolumbre tem boa relação.

Na Comissão de Desenvolvimento Regional, a relação é ainda mais direta. Do R$ 1,5 bilhão da CDR, R$ 838,5 milhões dependem da liberação do Ministério do Desenvolvimento Regional, comandado pelo conterrâneo de Alcolumbre, Waldez Goés.

Quando nomeou o ministro em 2023, Lula disse, citando nominalmente, que ele era uma indicação do atual presidente do Senado.

Se o Orçamento de 2027 mantiver os R$ 4 bilhões em emendas de comissão para o Senado, cada um dos 81 senadores poderia receber R$ 49,8 milhões, se os recursos fossem divididos igualmente.

Essa divisão é outro argumento utilizado por Alcolumbre para convencer senadores do PL. O presidente do Senado tem alertado que, além de ficar sem espaço nas comissões e na Mesa Diretora, o partido também perderá nas emendas de comissão.

Sem o PL, a divisão ficaria entre 52 senadores, o que, se a divisão for igual, deixa cada senador com uma cota de R$ 77,6 milhões em emendas de comissão.

Tereza quer unir mulheres e Marinho aposta em bancada do PL

Para furar a bolha de uma candidatura da direita, Tereza Cristina aposta em uma união da bancada feminina com a bandeira de ser a primeira mulher presidente do Senado na história.

Com críticas do bolsonarismo desde que anunciou sua candidatura, Tereza já atraiu o apoio de Damares Alves (Republicanos-DF) e Michelle Bolsonaro (PL-DF), que também já foram alvo de ataques do grupo.

Michelle, inclusive, não foi ao lançamento da candidatura de Rogério Marinho na sede de seu partido.

Procurado, Rogério Marinho disse que "desconhecia isso [os ataques], se solidariza, lamenta e desestimula qualquer tipo de comportamento como esse. Que a candidatura da Tereza Cristina é legítima e ambos têm um objetivo em comum de vencer o mesmo adversário".

Mesmo com o anúncio oficial da candidatura de Rogério Marinho na última semana, Tereza garante que está na disputa.

"Eu mantenho minha candidatura firme e forte. Temos cerca de 90 dias para dialogar e eu quero ser a primeira mulher presidente do Senado", afirmou Tereza ao g1.

Rogério Marinho, por outro lado, aposta numa candidatura que foi lançada com a presença de 30 senadores . Além de 26 quadros do PL, o evento contou os três senadores do Novo, dois do Republicanos e um do PP, partido de Tereza Cristina.

Além Michelle Bolsonaro, Eduardo Gomes, Zé Medeiros (PL-MT), Nicoletti (PL-RR) e Alex Diniz (PL-MG), foram quadros do PL ausentes no evento.

Apesar do número de parlamentares, há uma avaliação de quadros da direita de que Marinho está próximo do teto e que a candidatura de Tereza Cristina teria mais capacidade de atrair votos do Centrão e até de parlamentares ligados ao governo Lula.

articles.title: Rubio says Trump's war against Iran not 'necessarily popular' but needed to stop a nuclear threat
articles.summary: HOMESTEAD AIR RESERVE BASE, Fla. (AP) — Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran even if it was n...
articles.body:
HOMESTEAD AIR RESERVE BASE, Fla. (AP) — Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran even if it was not "necessarily popular" to safeguard the world from the country's nuclear ambitions.

He would not comment directly about the Republican wipeout in Tuesday's elections, which delivered a resounding rebuke to Trump. The unpopularity of the Iran war and its impact on gasoline prices and other parts of the economy helped Democrats seize control of Congress .

Asked about Vice President JD Vance's social media post last week that largely blamed the war for the Republican losses , Rubio told reporters that Trump "identified a very real threat" in Iran and worked to stop the Islamic Republic from pursuing a nuclear weapon.

"He addressed it even though oftentimes the right thing to do for the country — confronting difficult challenges for the security of our country — doing it isn't necessarily popular, but necessary," Rubio said in Florida before heading to a Group of 7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris.

America's top diplomat offered a robust defense of the more than eight-month-old war even as voters blamed Trump's policies for the hit to their pocketbooks, including higher energy prices that stemmed from disruptions to shipments in the Strait of Hormuz , a crucial waterway where one-fifth of the world's oil transited before the war.

Rubio and Vance offer differing comments on the war

Rubio's comments also put him at odds with Vance, who are both considered possible 2028 contenders. Asked in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday about potential candidates other than Vance, Trump named Rubio, saying that "I think Marco's great" but noting there was a "tremendous bench" in his Republican Party and that "maybe I'm better off not getting involved."

Trump told reporters Sunday that Vance was right about the war's impact on the election — other than that his vice president should have also insisted it was the correct choice to go to war.

"I can tell you if I had it to do again, this historically — for history — will go down as one of the best things we ever did," Trump said. "Because if they ever had a nuclear weapon, they would blow up the world."

Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%.

Asked on "60 Minutes" whether he would escalate the war following the elections, Trump said, "Well I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to."

Rubio says Iran talks aren't on the 'verge of a breakthrough'

With no clear administration strategy to wind down the conflict and the Middle East on edge over the possibility of a return to major hostilities, mediators are trying to revive talks between the sides.

Rubio said, "I wouldn't say we're at the verge of a breakthrough."

He reiterated that Trump prefers a diplomatic solution, but "right now, it hasn't been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic."

Trump is set to meet Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday, according to his official schedule.

The Associated Press has reported that Iran was reviewing proposals presented by chief mediator Qatar aimed at addressing differences with the United States about Tehran's nuclear program. But Iran was seen as unwilling to negotiate with the Trump administration over their atomic activities until the U.S. agrees to several core conditions that Tehran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement, officials have said.

Those include ending the U.S. blockade on Iran's ports , lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon.

While Rubio said there was no diplomatic breakthrough at hand, Trump told CNN in a phone interview Sunday that as long as the U.S. sees progress in negotiations with Tehran and they sign a "strong agreement," it's "highly unlikely it's going to be necessary" to resume strikes.

Trump said, however, that the U.S. had identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes.

The U.S. military, meanwhile, still has carried out limited strikes on Iran , including against its air defenses, at least twice over the past week. It also fired on and disabled a commercial ship Saturday that the U.S. says was trying to breach its naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Rubio acknowledged that the U.S. will take defensive actions if needed.

"If there's a clear and present threat to shipping or to our forces in the region, we have a right to defend ourselves," Rubio said.

Price reported from West Palm Beach, Fla.

articles.title: Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about making Dana White press secretary
articles.summary: Trump says he was joking when he offered Dana White the press secretary job, but confirmed the UFC boss is visiting the White House on Monday.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Sunday he was joking when he announced on social media that he had offered UFC boss Dana White the White House press secretary job and lined up a roster of fighters to serve as his assistants. "I will tell you, I was only kidding," Trump said when asked what prompted the pitch and whether he was serious. Trump pointed to the fighters he had named as White’s would-be assistants, saying the lineup should have given the joke away. "And you see a lot of rough faces there," he said. He also joked that some of the fighters came from "parts unknown." DANA WHITE DENIES AMERICA 250 UFC FIGHT AT WHITE HOUSE WILL BE 'POLITICAL,' 'NOT AT ALL' ABOUT POLITICS Trump said he thought White liked the idea and called him "a very capable guy." As for how the UFC boss might handle the job, Trump said, "You wouldn’t mess around with him so much." "But Dana is actually coming tomorrow," Trump said. He explained that the visit was for other reasons, saying he believed White already planned to be in Washington and would stop by to see him. TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY OUT OF THE JOB JUST DAYS AFTER ROCKY DEBUT Trump said some people took to the idea after he floated it. "And then people said, you know, that’s actually a pretty good idea," he said. The clarification came a day after Trump wrote on Truth Social that he had offered White the job. His post named UFC stars including Khabib Nurmagomedov, Islam Makhachev, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier and Amanda Nunes as prospective assistants. UFC STARS VISIT OVAL OFFICE, THANK PRESIDENT TRUMP FOR TRANSFORMING THE SPORT WITH HISTORIC WHITE HOUSE FIGHT "Dana, please take the job!" Trump wrote. White shared Trump’s post on his Instagram Story, along with a photo of himself behind the White House podium. He captioned the photo, "On to the next chapter." LEAVITT OPENS UP ON HELPING TRUMP FIND NEW PRESS SECRETARY AFTER ZACHARIA DEBACLE: 'WAS NOT FOR HER' The exchange came weeks after Katie Zacharia’s departure as press secretary. Zacharia had been tapped to succeed Karoline Leavitt, who left in August. Asked Oct. 23 about finding a replacement, Trump told reporters, "We’re in no rush." Trump and White have known each other for decades, dating back to the UFC’s early years, when Trump hosted fights at his Atlantic City property. White introduced Trump at the 2024 Republican National Convention and joined him on the White House South Lawn in June for UFC Freedom 250. KAROLINE LEAVITT REVEALS SHE’S ADVISED TRUMP ON WHITE HOUSE REPLACEMENT IN FINAL INTERVIEW AS PRESS SECRETARY White previously told Sports Business Journal in November 2024 that he had "no personal political aspirations" when asked about a possible role in Trump’s incoming administration. articles.title: Trump says his immigration crackdown ‘might be too tough’ after midterm losses
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday said his deportation policies might have been “too tough” and led to the GOP’s historic losses in this year’s elections. CBS News’s...
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday said his deportation policies might have been "too tough" and led to the GOP's historic losses in this year's elections.

CBS News's Ross Douthat asked the president on "60 Minutes" if his immigration policy lost his party the midterms.

"I think it both helped and hurt," Trump responded. "I think I got an A plus for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out, but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs that created one violation for breaking of the law, that was what they came into the country illegally."

"Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out," he continued. "And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people, working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

The president later went on to characterize his immigration policy as "too tough" and expressed interest in working across the aisle in the next Congress, when both chambers will be under Democratic control.

However, his recent decision to replace Susie Wiles with longtime adviser Stephen Miller, a hardliner on immigration , as White House chief of staff sends a different signal.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who has called out Miller's views on immigration, said on Friday that Trump "needs to rethink" Miller's appointment.

"It is a colossal mistake, and the last thing we need 72 hours after the a– whooping we got on Tuesday," Tillis told CNN on Friday.

Deportations have been a key focus for the second Trump administration – but it may have cost Trump politically.

In a July survey the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that 39 percent of respondents approved of the administration's handling of immigration, a 10-point drop from the start of his second term.

Americans have developed increasingly negative views of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), especially following the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti earlier this year in Minneapolis, which led to widespread backlash and protests nationwide .

Many Democratic lawmakers have condemned the president's action on immigration – but some Republican lawmakers have also shared their concerns and foresaw the president's immigration crackdown as a liability.

"Once you start deporting people who have otherwise been here without incident for 15, 20 years, that's a gray zone that I think where you find a lot of division of opinion," Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said in early October.

Cornyn was up for re-election but lost the Republican primary to Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. He was defeated on Tuesday by the now Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas), who was critical of ICE's actions throughout his campaign.

"We need Immigration and Customs Enforcement in this country, but that's not what we're seeing," Talarico said at a town hall in October. "What we've seen over the last year is a secret police force, and that's what we don't want in this country."

President Trump said on Sunday that he offered UFC CEO Dana White the White House press secretary role as a joke.

“I will tell you, I was only kidding,” Trump told reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida. “But Dana loves the idea, and there’s only one Dana, and he’s great.”

The president then appeared to reference either his original announcement or a cartoon video he posted to Truth Social earlier Sunday, which featured White and a number of UFC fighters in the White House briefing room. The video depicts the fighters attacking reporters.

“Of course, I was kidding. And you can see that, because they put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all gonna come with them. But it was, it was just a little fun,” Trump added, before noting that White would be arriving in Washington, D.C., Monday and planned to speak with the president about the role.

He announced White’s job offer in a Saturday Truth Social post , writing, “I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States.”

“I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris,” the president continued. “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left.”

The White House has yet to find a permanent replacement for Karoline Leavitt, who departed her role earlier this year.

Katie Zacharia, a political commentator, spent a short, controversial 5 days in the role, which ended after some accused Zacharia of misrepresenting her legal credentials.

"I think it both helped and hurt," Trump answered. "I think I got an A-plus for closing up the border…I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out."

In the extended interview posted online , Trump added, "We had 25 million people come in through Biden over a four-year period, and many of those people were — as you know, they were from prisons, they were drug dealers, they were from mental institutions."

However, Trump conceded that many illegal immigrants within the country were "good" people, which likely led to his policies facing backlash.

"But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that — that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And in some cases, paying taxes. And there's a large group of people who think that they should be allowed to stay."

articles.body:
President Trump said during a Sunday appearance on “60 minutes” that the “hatred between” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin is one of the primary obstacles toward resolving the Russia-Ukraine war.

CBS News’s Ross Douthat questioned Trump about his promise to end the Russia-Ukraine war , a claim he touted during his most recent campaign run. Douthat asked the president what the biggest obstacle to peace has been for the war, which is now almost in its fifth year.

“It was the hatred between Zelensky and Putin. If I had been president that war would’ve never started. Zero chance. But it did start. So I inherited that war. I believe we’re very close to making a deal,” Trump responded.

Douthat then asked the president if there was one party he trusted more than the other.

“I’d rather not say, but I get along with both. I believe that that war is going to end, and it’s going to end soon. And the only reason it’s going to end is because of me. There is tremendous hatred between President Putin and President Zelensky,” Trump added.

Douthat told the president that Zelensky’s feelings might be understandable since it was Russia that invaded Ukraine.

“Well, it is. But when they had their first meeting there was great disrespect shown to Russia. So I’m not going to say anything,” Trump said. “Let’s put it this way: the war never happened during my four years, and it was never going to happen, even though it was the apple of President Putin’s eye.”

The president in recent months has blamed the Russia-Ukraine war for rising fuel costs, which posed a significant political problem for the GOP heading into the midterms and may have contributed to Tuesday’s “blue wave.”

Last month, Trump announced that both countries agreed to an energy ceasefire in a Truth Social post. Shortly after, however, Russia struck a power plant in eastern Ukraine.

In an effort to alleviate the global oil and gas markets, which have been strained by the war in Iran, the president also announced a diesel diel with Russia , drawing sharp criticism from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers .

Sen. Thom Tillis (R- N.C.) called the agreement “beyond irresponsible.”

Zelensky in response told NBC News’s Kristen Welker, “If United States will support Putin, I mean, it’s unbelievable, it’s tragedy, it’s historic mistake and big tragedy.”

articles.body:
Erika Kirk, the widow of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, condemned comedians and political commentators for joking about political violence after Dave Chappelle said during a stand-up performance that he had been in a “good mood” since her husband’s assassination.

“To see leftist podcasters, comedians, and commentators laugh about political assassination as though it’s entertainment and the destruction of a human life is a punchline, is beyond disgusting,” Erika Kirk wrote in a post on the social platform X .

She did not name Chapelle in her post on the social platform X, but criticized those who have made light of her husband’s killing.

“My husband, Charlie Kirk, was killed in an act of political violence, something our two children and I will live with every day for the rest of our lives,” she continued.

Charlie Kirk, the founder of Turning Point USA and a prominent ally of President Trump, was fatally shot while speaking at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. He was 31.

“A culture that laughs at assassination is one of profound moral decay. It threatens the very foundation of our country and the principles that hold our democracy together,” his widow wrote on X. “You do not have to agree with someone’s politics to recognize the value of their life. This should not be so hard. Political violence must never be something this country tolerates, excuses, or celebrates.”

Chappelle made the remark Saturday during a sold-out show at Madison Square Garden in New York City, according to footage circulating on social media.

“I feel f–ed up saying this. It’s scary being a public speaker,” Chapelle told the audience. “Ever since that guy Charlie Kirk got murdered — and I shouldn’t say this publicly — but, I feel better.”

Chapelle previously discussed Kirk’s killing in his Netflix comedy special The Unstoppable , released three months after the shooting. At the time, he said the assassination had shaken him as someone who also speaks publicly for a living.

“If you talk for a living and see Charlie Kirk get murdered that way, Imma be honest,” he said. “I was shook.”

articles.title: Bernie Sanders warns Democrats not to spend all their time investigating Trump
articles.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders warned Democrats not to spend all their time investigating the Trump administration, urging the party to prioritize affordability and working-class families.
articles.body: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Democrats should hold President Donald Trump accountable after taking control of the House and Senate in January, but warned the party not to spend too much time on probing the president and his allies. During an appearance on NBC News' "Meet the Press," the senator said it is still important to investigate Trump administration officials for alleged corruption and illegal activity, but stressed that the priority should be tackling affordability and supporting working-class families. Asked by host Kristen Welker if he believes that spending two years investigating Trump and his officials could jeopardize the mandate to lower prices and make life more affordable, Sanders replied, "Yes, I do." "Do we want to hold the Trump administration accountable for their corruption, for their illegal, unconstitutional actions? Absolutely," Sanders said. DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS However, Sanders said that Democrats "cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump." "At the end of the day, when you’ve got the highest rate of childhood poverty in America, of any major country, when 20% of our seniors are trying to survive on $15,000 a year, when people are scared to death that Elon Musk and the other billionaires are pushing AI down our throats with cataclysmic impacts on the economy, our privacy rights, on our health, and — and imposing an existential threat to humanity, we cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump," he said. "We’ve got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives," Sanders continued. Democrats campaigned on affordability ahead of the midterms, blaming the Trump administration for the soaring costs of gas, groceries, housing and healthcare. Candidates linked the rise in costs, in part, to the U.S. military's war on Iran and Trump's tariffs on countries around the world. The Iran war, which Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other allies partially attributed to Republicans' midterm losses, led to surging fuel prices. Gas prices are nearly $1 per gallon higher than they were a year ago, according to AAA, which reported that the national average was $4.02 per gallon as of Sunday. But after securing the majority in both chambers of Congress following last week's elections, several Democrats promised to use the power of the subpoena and investigate current and former Trump officials once they are sworn in. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH Incoming House Oversight Committee leader Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., on Sunday warned that Democrats could investigate Trump's pardons as well as allies of the president, including tech executive Elon Musk and newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. Garcia also said last week that Oversight Democrats are "ready to take on the crooks, the con men, and the Trump crime family." "Lawyer up," he added. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to be the next House Speaker, also said last week that Democrats are "going to bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country." "Because if you have people in high office who are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends or their donors, then they’re not focused on making life better for the American people. But House Democrats will put the American people first," he continued. Sanders said on Sunday that the election was not just about voters wanting to stop the Trump administration’s policies. "And what the American people are saying: 'Look, we are working long hours. We’re worried about our kids. We can’t afford healthcare. We can’t afford housing. Meanwhile, the wealthiest people in America have never, ever had it so good.' And right now is the moment where the Democrats have got to stand up to big money, create an economy and a government that works for all of us," Sanders said. The Vermont senator also accused Trump of being "mentally unbalanced" and "erratic," but acknowledged that the president is "a good politician" and "not stupid" who Democrats may be able to work with on economic and healthcare issues. "Trump is many things. I personally believe he is mentally unbalanced, erratic, but he’s not stupid, and he is a good politician. And I think, when Trump looks out in the world and he sees millions of people working for starvation wages, he might not be unsympathetic to raising the minimum wage to a living wage. He would love, I think, to take credit for doing what every other major country does, guaranteeing healthcare to all people. Do I think we can work with Trump? Maybe. I’m, by no means, guaranteeing it. But it is certainly worth the effort," he said.

articles.title: Rubio says war on Iran unpopular but ‘necessary’ to stop nuclear threat
articles.summary: US secretary of state says Iran’s negotiation demands are ‘outrageous and ridiculous, and really not realistic’.
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran to safeguard the world from Tehran’s nuclear ambitions.

Rubio told reporters in Florida on Sunday that Trump “identified a very real threat” in Iran and had worked to stop it from pursuing a nuclear weapon.

Trump addressed “difficult challenges for the security of our country – doing it isn’t necessarily popular, but necessary”, Rubio added.

On diplomatic efforts to end the war, Rubio said, “I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough”. He added that although Trump prefers a diplomatic solution, Iranian demands are “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic”.

Rubio comments came after Trump had said that “a lot of people didn’t like” Vice President JD Vance recent comments blaming the US-led war on Iran for the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in last week’s US midterm elections.

Trump said that although he mostly agreed with Vance, he did not regret the decision to go to war against Iran. It “will go down as one of the best things we ever did”, he said, adding that if Tehran were to have a nuclear weapon, “they would blow up the world”.

Trump also told CNN in a phone interview on Sunday that as long as Washington sees progress in negotiations with Tehran and they sign a “strong agreement”, it is “highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary” for the US to resume strikes.

For Iran’s part, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that it was “time for the White House to make its own” decision on the war.

“American voters have made their choice,” Araghchi wrote on X, referring to the midterm election results.

He added that Tehran’s “2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results”.

“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

Iran has offered to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within two days if the United States meets its conditions.

Trump is set to meet Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House on Monday, according to his official schedule.

Tehran is reviewing proposals presented by Qatar aimed at addressing differences with Washington, according to the Associated Press news agency.

In recent days, Rubio has also denied “unfounded” speculation that he was quitting as the top US diplomat to run for higher office in 2028.

articles.title: Trump team interprets midterms debacle as a cue to go harder, further, faster
articles.summary: It’s as if the midterms never happened.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is heading into this week's impeachment showdown over Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — the first major test of the president's power after his election debacle — with a clear warning that it plans to use executive authority with even greater force in the new political era.

There's little sense of contrition or acknowledgment that Americans voted to impose restraints on President Donald Trump. The unequivocal White House response was instead represented by the appointment of Stephen Miller , the architect of many of Trump's most aggressive policies, as White House chief of staff .

Attorney General Todd Blanche spelled out the message on CNN on Sunday morning, saying Democrats who plan to employ constitutional prerogatives to investigate the administration should be "worried" after Trump demanded Department of Justice criminal probes into their activity.

In dueling interviews on "State of the Union," the administration and its critics laid down political battle lines for next year.

"Before they're even in power, they're already talking about investigations and impeachments, with no basis, no facts, just out there running around," Blanche told CNN's Dana Bash. "That should be something that President Trump is very concerned about, and certainly I am as well."

But Robert Garcia , the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, warned the new Democratic Congress would not cow before a "threat" from Blanche. "He's trying to stop us from doing real oversight. … The Constitution makes it very clear that it's our job in the Congress to conduct oversight of the executive and the administration," Garcia said.

Hegseth impeachment will showcase GOP anger with Trump

But the first confrontation, over a potential House of Representatives vote to impeach Hegseth, will do more to test how the midterm wipeout has hurt Trump's authority among Republicans than Democrats' capacity to restrain him.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie plans to bring articles of impeachment against Hegseth this week as the Pentagon chief intensifies a vehement campaign to keep his job despite criticism of his conduct of the Iran war.

There are growing suggestions that even many Republicans would like the combative Hegseth gone, especially after Rep. James Comer expressed reservations about him last week. Comer, unlike his fellow Kentuckian Massie, who was beaten by a pro-Trump rival in his primary, remains loyal to the president.

The White House is standing by Hegseth, so far. Trump told reporters last week his defense secretary was doing "a very good job." And Hegseth reacted to Miller's promotion by portraying him as a fellow fighter against the president's enemies with a social media post reading "Stand. Fight."

Hegseth's viability, however, could be undermined by a strong vote against him by GOP members. Those who've lost their jobs amid public fury over Iran may have little incentive to stand strong with him and the president. It seems unlikely that there will be the two-thirds majority in the Senate needed to convict and remove Hegseth from office in an impeachment trial. But he's made few friends in the Senate, and these are volatile political days.

The Hegseth impeachment drama will unfold against the last rites of the lame-duck Republican-led Congress, which must pass a funding bill by December 11 to keep the government open. The defense secretary's controversial presence may also complicate the Senate passage of a critical defense spending bill.

Battle lines drawn over Congress vs. White House confrontation

In the first days after the Democrats' midterm rout, Trump seemed subdued. But now it's clear the White House wants a fight.

Asked on Sunday's edition of CBS' "60 Minutes" whether he could ever forgive his enemies, Trump answered: "I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will."

On Saturday, Trump complained on Truth Social that Democrats had sent threatening letters to Republicans and donors and ordered the Justice Department to investigate them, while claiming "these extortionists" should be imprisoned.

Last week, Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal issued a warning to individuals, companies and government agencies to cooperate with investigations into "cryptocurrency; corruption involving the Trump Administration's self-enrichment and national security threats; rampant misconduct by federal immigration agents; Big Tech and other corporate enablers; and the Trump Administration's lawless abuse of power."

Blumenthal said that if the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations did not get responses by January, the new Congress would act. Also last week, Garcia said in a video that "crooks, the con men and the Trump crime family" need to "lawyer up."

Blanche argued that such rhetoric goes too far.

"You have an incoming chairman threatening … they're not even in charge yet — saying, 'Lawyer up' to anybody in particular. So, if that doesn't bother you, if that doesn't bother your viewers, then we really need to kind of wake up in this country, because it certainly bothers me," Blanche told CNN.

The attorney general said Garcia's complaints about his own vow to represent officials targeted by congressional investigations showed "a remarkable lack of understanding of how government works." He added: "I would be very worried if I was a member on that committee."

But Garcia hit back. "Quite frankly, what Todd Blanche is doing right now is a threat," he said on "State of the Union."

"He is threatening our committee. He's trying to stop us from doing real oversight," the California Democrat said of Blanche, arguing that "all he wants to do is protect Donald Trump, is protect Donald Trump's Cabinet and administration officials."

Democrats have their own risks heading into new era

The appearances by Blanche and Garcia gave a preview of Washington next year and the risks both parties are likely to take during Trump's last two years in office.

The administration is implying that any true oversight of the administration is illegitimate; what Trump called "Weaponization and Lawfare" on Truth Social. This strategy was successful when Trump leveraged investigations into his company, his efforts to overturn the 2020 election and his retention of classified material into a narrative of political persecution that unified Republicans and helped him to reclaim the presidency in 2024. It's not surprising that he's trying to turn the same trick now, since Blanche, then one of his top personal lawyers, was a chief architect of his legal fight.

The Republicans' midterm election defeat was about many things: the Iran war, the cost of living, soaring gas prices, public distaste with immigration crackdowns, and a sense Trump pursues his own interests over the country's. But the administration is showing it plans to wring every ounce of power from Trump's term.

Increasingly, top officials are speaking in rather apocalyptic terms. As he professed his "total devotion" and "absolute loyalty" to Trump at Mar-a-Lago on Friday, Miller warned that if it weren't for the president, "the United States of America would not exist right now." In his videos fighting for his job, Hegseth pledges to defend the republic against "all enemies, foreign and domestic." All this implies the administration sees some domestic opponents as bent on destroying the country — which just voted in a democratic election to repudiate its current rulers.

Democratic Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, who won a stunning upset victory in Kansas, expressed concern about the administration's response to the elections. He described Miller's appointment as "almost a doubling down" and told CNN that "people in my state, which is typically a pretty red state, have said, 'This is not OK. This is not who we are.'"

But the aftermath of the elections also underscores the challenges facing the incoming Democratic majority. While Democrats made investigating Trump's alleged corruption a centerpiece of their campaigns, and therefore have a mandate, voters primarily issued a cry for help with the cost of living. Acting on such concerns will be difficult enough, since Trump is armed with a presidential veto. A bitter climate of investigations could poison any hope of cooperation.

Xochitl Hinojosa, a CNN political commentator and former senior Justice Department official, told Bash she is "worried the Democrats will overreach."

Hinojosa added: "I do think that there needs to be some oversight, because there have been no checks on this administration whatsoever. But both parties need to realize that the voters said, 'We do not want infighting. We do not want Republicans and Democrats going at each other. What we want is people to deliver results.'"

Sunday's fierce political exchanges show how hard that will be.

articles.title: Sánchez explica por qué Trump tiene tanta manía a España: “Una reflexión, nada científico”
articles.standfirst: Lo comenta en el pódcast Memorias de Pez
articles.summary: Lo comenta en el pódcast Memorias de Pez
articles.body: L as relaciones entre Estados Unidos y la Unión Europea atraviesan uno de sus momentos más delicados y ha sido el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, quien ha metido el dedo en la llaga en una entrevista en el pódcast de YouTube 'Memorias de Pez'. Abordó cuestiones de geopolítica internacional como el conflicto del Sáhara, las relaciones con China, la inteligencia artificial y, cómo no, la figura de Donald Trump, con quien mantiene un largo historial de desencuentros políticos. Pero concretamente Sánchez aseguró que tanto España como la Unión Europea intentan mantener unas relaciones "productivas" con Washington pese a "lo impredecible" del actual inquilino de la Casa Blanca. Una situación que conoce de primera mano tras años siendo uno de los objetivos habituales de las críticas de Trump, especialmente a raíz de su rechazo a elevar el gasto en Defensa hasta el 5% del PIB, como reclama Estados Unidos. Sánchez planteó una reflexión sobre el origen del deterioro de las relaciones transatlánticas amparándose en lo que llamó una "reflexión, nada científico". "La pregunta que me surge es cuánto hay de estructural en el malestar que Trump manifiesta y cuánto hay de personal, de su forma de entender la política", añadió a su explicación. Y su conclusión fue contundente. "Yo diría que hay un 70% personal en la explicación de por qué están las cosas frías entre Estados Unidos y la Unión Europea, y un 30% de cuestiones estructurales que ambas partes deben abordar", sostuvo. Sánchez fue un paso más allá y puso el foco en la necesidad de revisar el actual Pacto Atlántico surgido tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial y reforzado con el Plan Marshall. En su opinión, Europa debe ganar peso tanto en el ámbito económico como en el de la defensa. Como ejemplo, el presidente destacó el papel limitado que, a su juicio, tiene la Unión Europea dentro de la OTAN. "A mí me llama la atención cómo la Unión Europea no participa en las cumbres de la OTAN. Está invitada a las cenas de líderes, pero no a la toma de decisiones", afirmó.

articles.title: The stoning of Stephen Miller, now running the Trump White House
articles.summary: Trump's decision to name Stephen Miller his new chief of staff sparked an unprecedented media firestorm, as critics quickly targeted his hardline immigration record and influence over the president's agenda.
articles.body: When Donald Trump made the stunning announcement that Stephen Miller is his new chief of staff–preempting the New York Times by a few minutes–I literally said: "Watch for a barrage of negative Miller stories in the next couple of days." I was wrong. It was the next couple of hours. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH MS NOW anchor Katy Tur said: "Donald Trump’s whole immigration agenda is Stephen Miller, and for Stephen Miller, it has always been absolutist: do whatever is necessary, as much as we can possibly do, be as cruel as possible as a warning sign for anybody who might want to come over." WHITE HOUSE SHAKEUP CONTINUES WITH NEW DEPARTURE FROM TRUMP ADMINISTRATION "Stephen Miller, one of his most notorious staffers, will instead be taking over as chief of staff," CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins said from the White House driveway, adding: "He was one of two staffers, including Kristi Noem, who came out after Alex Pretti was killed in Minneapolis and called him a domestic terrorist." Embed: That New York Times story: "Miller, a deeply ideological Trump loyalist, has been the architect of some of the most polarizing domestic policies in Mr. Trump’s second term." The conservative Federalist cited a past Miller comment on mass deportations: "At every turn illegal aliens have always been treated better than Americans." And then there are the Democrats. Rep. Robert Garcia, the expected incoming House Oversight chairman, said: "Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families… Stephen Miller should lawyer up." Oh, and incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries called him "a dangerous xenophobe." Of course, it’s a huge story, and should be covered as such. It’s about his record, and, putting aside the adjectives, it’s fair game. My purpose here is not to either defend or criticize Miller, who has been one of Trump’s most powerful aides since the first term. Miller is, without question, one of the hardest of hardliners. I cannot remember this kind of all-out artillery attack, seconds after a top White House appointment was announced. I don’t think anything else comes close. And the sheer velocity and global reach of this negativity is being fueled in the digital battleground of social media. That evening was just the first line of shock troops, who struck as soon as Trump announced that Miller would replace Susie Wiles, who has battled breast cancer, as his top aide. By the next morning, the cavalry had arrived. The Wall Street Journal called Miller an "advocate of the no-holds-barred style of governing that delighted the president’s most die-hard MAGA supporters—and was repudiated by much of the rest of the country on Election Day." Axios, describing Miller’s view of nearly unlimited presidential powers, said of Trump: "He's prepping for war, and sees Miller as a brass-knuckle general and tactical expert impervious to criticism or traditional restraints." The New York Post, headlining the old beer ad "It’s Miller Time," said that choosing the "pugnacious" official "removes almost all hope that the nation’s partisan warfare will ease after the elections." The president is "going to bring his pit bull along." TRUMP NAMES STEPHEN MILLER NEW WHITE HOUSE CHIEF OF STAFF, REPLACING SUSIE WILES The Times, in its pair of stories, played some of the 41-year-old Miller’s greatest hits. "Those include separation of migrant families at the border; the 2017 Muslim travel ban, directing the government to stifle critics of Mr. Trump; the ending of nearly all U.S. refugee programs; the widespread pressure campaign against American universities; extrajudicial boat strikes that have killed hundreds; and purges of officials deemed insufficiently loyal to Mr. Trump." Miller also unleashed the military, "pitting masked, heavily armed immigration agents against residents of cities like Minneapolis and Chicago." Fact-check: True. Maureen Dowd, not to be outdone, denounced the "gaudy, corrupt, vice-ridden, heartless rule, we have been living in Trumpsville. The demonic Trump conjured an American hell." Miller hasn’t exactly stayed silent. He said Trump is "the most transformative political leader" in our history and has "single-handedly saved America from those who would destroy it." A day after the election, Miller led a call about pushing forward with mass deportations and, the Times reports, did not even mention the Democratic avalanche that was partially a protest against such policies. The president says he loves watching the combative Miller on TV–a key credential for any Trump staffer. Miller is certain to back Trump’s assaults on the mainstream media, ranging from denunciations and lawsuits to whether the press corps should be evicted from the White House. Shortly before the election, Miller said on Elon Musk’s X that the Democrats have nominated candidates "who are all extremist, freaks and America-hating lunatics." Miller urged voters to "send a message to the corrupt media, corrupt Democrats and corrupt left-wing politicians who want to steal your future." It’s not hard to see why Miller has a target on his back. But imagine that Miller, who also urged his boss to wind down the Iran war, never joined the administration. Wouldn’t Trump still have pursued all these tough policies, starting with mass deportation? Clearly, it’s the commander-in-chief who decides. TRUMP ‘HOLDS ALL THE CARDS’ IN WAR AGAINST IRAN’S REGIME, WHITE HOUSE SAYS Other top aides and Cabinet secretaries have certainly been raked over the coals. The media weren’t kind to Karl Rove, dubbed "Bush’s brain," the strategist who was investigated in a CIA leak case but never charged. Some were accused of being too close to the industries they regulated. Ronald Reagan’s Interior secretary James Watt ripped the environmental movement as a clash between "liberals and Americans," and the Sierra Club collected more than 1 million signatures seeking his ouster. But none of them were pummeled with the fierce intensity that has enveloped Miller. As for the coming investigations, Todd Blanche announced that "the chief of staff already has a lawyer. The attorney general of the United States and the Justice Department." With those words, the AG confirmed again that his department serves as the personal law firm of Trump and his acolytes. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Look, Stephen Miller is a brawler, the opposition party is spoiling for a fight, and that should provide the press and public with plenty of pounding in the political ring. But while Miller is now the most important staffer of Donald Trump’s last two years in office, remember, he is still a staffer.

articles.title: Trump says his immigration policy ‘too tough’ for voters
articles.summary: Trump concedes some voters were unhappy with his administration’s controversial deportation drive.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has said his immigration policy may have been too extreme for voters, conceding that his deportation policy had damaged his Republican Party’s performance in the last week’s midterm elections.

During his first television interview since his party lost control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate last week, Trump said some voters were unhappy with his administration’s controversial deportation drive, which led to widespread protests .

“I think it might be too tough,” he told CBS’s 60 Minutes programme, which aired on Sunday.

He said he may be able to work with the new Democratic-controlled Congress on some kind of immigration agreement.

“The deal would be we would work something out,” he said, adding, “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

The interview was aired after he appointed Stephen Miller, the chief architect of his hardline immigration policy, to replace Susie Wiles as his White House chief of staff, prompting questions about the direction of his immigration policy.

In a post on X, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said, “Trump says his immigration crackdown went too far”, adding, “Apparently, his solution was to put the man responsible for it in charge of the White House. That’s not a course correction. That’s a promotion.”

Trump had promised an immigration crackdown during his campaign to return to office, blaming undocumented migrant “killers” and “drug dealers” for soaring crime.

Extensive operations to detain and deport immigrants were launched in multiple US cities, causing arrests to soar.

Two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – were killed by federal officers during protests against the operations.

Democrats have said oversight of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Department of Homeland Security is a priority for the new Congress.

During his interview, Trump said a moderate immigration deal would still deport criminals, but allow “good people” who had lived and worked in the country “paying taxes” to stay.

articles.title: Border Dem poised to wield ICE purse strings rejects socialist ‘defund’ push
articles.summary: Rep. Henry Cuellar rejects the Abolish ICE movement, saying most Democrats oppose defunding the agency but want stronger oversight and rail guards.
articles.body: A longtime Democratic House member representing a southern border district said Immigration and Customs Enforcement is not going anywhere as "Abolish ICE" became a rallying cry for more than a dozen progressive Democrats elected or reelected in the midterms. While the elections brought a new class of Democratic Socialists of America members to Congress, Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital that they make up just "one part of the spectrum" and that there are many "blue dogs" like himself who value strong border and immigration policies. "I don't believe in defunding ICE and I think the majority of the Democrats do not believe defunding ICE, but there are serious rail guards we need put on ICE," Cuellar said. Cuellar also warned Democrats against returning to the Biden administration’s border policies. DEM REP SETH MOULTON SAYS PARTY HAS NO IMMIGRATION PLAN, IS ONLY ‘OPPOSITION TO TRUMP’ "We just can't open up the border and just say anybody that wants to claim asylum can come to the borders. That policy under Biden administration — I hope that every Democrat running for national office doesn't do that anymore," Cuellar said. Cuellar, who is currently the ranking member of the Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee, is poised to become chairman, giving him significant influence over how funding for ICE is allocated. The congressman's district includes Laredo, where Border Patrol has a major presence. Cuellar has repeatedly broken with his party on immigration enforcement, including voting with Republicans in January to approve a DHS funding bill that included billions for ICE, though he later opposed a $70 billion Republican-backed enforcement package over concerns about oversight. Cuellar has criticized ICE for pursuing immigrants without criminal records, even though federal law allows the agency to arrest people for civil immigration violations. He has also called for greater oversight of the agency. "Anybody that thinks that what ICE is doing, going after nuns, going after pastors, going after dreamers, they think that's normal? I don't think Cuellar said, attributing the blue wave in Texas to Trump's immigration enforcement tactics. The Abolish ICE movement became a flashpoint for the Trump administration amid sweeping immigration enforcement operations in major cities including Minneapolis, Los Angeles, Chicago and New Orleans. The operations have resulted in more than 1.3 million arrests and 1.2 million illegal immigrants being deported or leaving the country, according to the White House. Democrats and immigrant rights activists have criticized ICE's tactics, which include targeting courthouses, churches and job sites, as well as conditions in detention centers. The agency has also faced fierce backlash over the fatal shootings of two American citizens by ICE agents in Minnesota just weeks apart in January 2026. In the months that followed, Democratic governors in New York, California, Connecticut, Illinois, Maryland and Minnesota signed laws restricting local and state cooperation with federal immigration officials. DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE Meanwhile, ICE’s partnerships with Texas authorities have expanded through 287(g) agreements that allow local officers to assist with immigration enforcement, jail screening and administrative warrants. Texas law now requires most county sheriffs to seek these agreements. Cuellar said local law enforcement should have a limited role: "I think the local sheriff should report somebody that’s there illegally. I think that’s it. But anything beyond that, I think we need to have a discussion," Cuellar told Fox News Digital. Like Cuellar, Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has been highly critical of ICE's tactics. At a rally in January, she criticized Gov. Greg Abbott for directing state agencies to make Texas land and facilities available for federal immigration detention. During her time in the state House, Hinojosa voted against a 2017 bill requiring local law enforcement to cooperate with federal agencies. But Hinojosa has never called for Texas to follow New York and other blue states' lead in ending all cooperation with ICE. "She is from the border from Brownsville," Cuellar said. "I haven't heard her say that she supports the defunding ICE. I don't think she has said that. Does she probably believe in transparency and rail guards for ICE? Again, I don't want to speak for her, but I think she does." Hinojosa has also sharply criticized Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, calling the operation a political "grandstand." Operation Lone Star launched in March 2021 amid a sharp rise in border encounters that began in 2020 and accelerated after President Joe Biden took office. The operation deployed Texas DPS officers, National Guard troops and local law enforcement to combat illegal crossings, human smuggling and drug trafficking before expanding to include state arrests and prosecutions for illegal entry, construction of border barriers and migrant transportation. In a recent CBS interview, former Border Patrol Chief Raul Ortiz said the Biden administration sent mixed messages to migrants and accused some officials of "embracing the chaos and crisis" at the southern border. DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR Cuellar agreed with Ortiz's assessment that the Biden administration didn't do its job securing the border. "The Biden Administration had it wrong," Cuellar said. Cuellar also criticized Abbott's deployment of Operation Lone Star, pointing to a January 2024 standoff in Eagle Pass, where Texas authorities seized control of Shelby Park and restricted Border Patrol’s access. "You still got to work with border patrol, regardless if it's a Democrat or Republican at the White House itself," Cuellar said. "So I can understand why there was that criticism, but still the Governor should have done a better job working with us at the federal level. And I hope that this new governor — and I think she will — work with us." Cuellar said there needs to be balance and nuance in how immigration policy is carried out and that he wants to work with Trump and Republicans over the next two years. "There are Democrats who are willing to work with the administration, with President Trump, but it takes two to have a deal," Cuellar said. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement to Fox News Digital that deportations will continue. We are focused on getting the job done and enthusiastically partner with any official dedicated to achieving that goal," CBP Assistant Commissioner Hilton Beckham said in a statement to Fox News Digital. articles.title: Qatar PM to meet Trump: What’s the latest on US-Iran negotiations?
articles.summary: Iran has put forward a two-day proposal developed with Qatari mediators that Washington is examining.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump is set to hold talks with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani behind closed doors at the White House on Monday, amid ongoing diplomatic efforts to bridge differences over Iran ’s nuclear programme and the terms for ending the conflict.

An unnamed US official told the Reuters news agency that Vice President JD Vance is also scheduled to hold talks with Sheikh Mohammed, who also serves as foreign minister and has been known to act as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran.

Iran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions by Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on Iran.

Here is a look at where diplomatic efforts stand before the meeting:

Iran offered the US a new nuclear and peace proposal via Qatari mediators on Thursday, to be discussed only after Washington meets Tehran’s seven demands. The US is examining the proposal.

Iran has been unwilling to hold negotiations over its atomic activities with the Trump administration until the latter agrees to several core conditions that Tehran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement.

Tehran has long maintained that its nuclear programme is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9kg (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60 percent purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90 percent.

Iran’s enrichment boost came after Trump withdrew from the nuclear deal in 2018. Signed under President Barack Obama, the deal had capped enrichment at below 3.67 percent.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the US resumes attacks.

Speaking to Al Jazeera last month, Araghchi said Tehran’s two-day proposal was developed with Qatari mediators and based on the seven-day plan Iran announced at the UN General Assembly in September.

“On day one, the US implements a set of measures. On day two, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen, and navigation will be restored to what it used to be,” he said.

Tehran’s demands include lifting the sanctions Washington imposed on Iran after the collapse of a memorandum of understanding, signed in Islamabad, Pakistan, in June, reducing the US military presence in the region, reinstating the oil waivers granted in June as part of the MoU and releasing frozen Iranian funds, including those held in Qatar.

Tehran also requested that the new shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, worked out by Iran and Oman be formally recognised and that all other routes be closed. Finally, it demanded ending the war on all fronts, including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon .

Araghchi held talks with 12 regional counterparts over 48 hours last week, calling for a regional security arrangement free from the involvement of extra-regional powers. Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, warned Trump on Saturday against renewed attacks, saying: “Start war and you will face a devastating response.”

Trump on Sunday warned that Washington had identified additional targets in Iran should military action resume, but said it was “highly unlikely” to ‌launch new strikes if negotiations yielded a strong agreement.

Sheikh Mohammed said mediation efforts continue and that the US has intentions and willingness to “take steps towards finding a solution”, after Trump confirmed on Friday that the White House was talking to Iranian representatives and that the team had “made a lot of progress with Iran”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said negotiations with Iran had not made progress. He told reporters in Florida on Sunday that while the war was unpopular, Trump “ identified a very real threat ” in Iran and had worked to stop it from pursuing a nuclear weapon.

Rubio added that although the US president prefers a diplomatic solution, Iranian demands are “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic”.

“I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough,” he added.

US media reported that Trump was being pressed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Central Command (CENTCOM) commander Brad Cooper to resume attacks against Iran .

Axios quoted a US official as saying CENTCOM was preparing for the resumption of major military operations in Iran, and that it was just waiting for orders from Washington.

On Thursday, Trump told reporters the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts.

Trump warned that US forces have three aircraft carriers stationed in the region “fully locked and loaded”, ready to continue strikes if need be. He said the US identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes.

The US military, meanwhile, has carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defences, at least twice over the past week. It also fired on a commercial ship and disabled it on Saturday, which the US said was trying to breach its naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Rubio said Washington would take “defensive” actions if needed. “If there’s a clear and present threat to shipping or to our forces in the region, we have a right to defend ourselves,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Aerospace Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Sunday made threats that echoed those of the Iranian foreign minister and said weapons have been “secured for years to come”.

IRGC Brigadier-General Ali Belali said in a statement on Telegram that “the armed forces are at the ready, and if the enemy makes a mistake, Iran’s response will be devastating and severe.”
